title: The sad saga of Dr. Iggy Agbayani
primary_topics: The conviction, jailing, and Oct 5 jail-death (cardiac arrest, four-and-a-half months into confinement) of orthopedic surgeon Dr. Benigno 'Iggy' Agbayani Jr. for 'reckless imprudence resulting in serious physical injuries'

Procedural collapse of his appeals: RTC appeal dismissed for counsel's failure to file appeal memorandum within the 15-day reglementary period despite extension; CA dismissed for failure to append required documents; SC Third Division denied via unsigned extended resolution (UER) for the same documentary failure
Author's critique: he would have voted (if still incumbent) to remand on the non-sterilization fact issue -- placing himself in the liberal school of jurisprudence vs the verba legis majority

Doctrinal clarification to calm medical professionals: the UER did not create a precedent on doctor criminal liability for reckless imprudence -- UERs as a rule do not create precedents; only signed decisions and resolutions do

Endorsement of Estelito P. Mendoza's posthumous retention by the family to clear Dr. Agbayani's name, with the qualification that the offended party (Atty. Hofileña Jr.) also deserves justice (not vengeance)
sub_topics: Conviction date and basis: July 29, 2013, Metropolitan Trial Court of Manila -- 'reckless imprudence resulting in serious physical injuries' for arthroscopy on Atty. Saul Q. Hofileña Jr.'s left knee using a non-sterilized arthroscope
RTC-Manila dismissal of his appeal for counsel's failure to file an appeal memorandum within 15-day reglementary period despite extension

CA junked his appeal for 'failure to append to his petition' the required documents under the Rules of Court (witnesses' affidavits, prosecution evidence, all pleadings filed before the lower courts, etc.)

SC Third Division UER (June 23, 2021) denied his petition for review for counsel's repeated failure to submit the required documents -- but shortened his imprisonment to 'one month and one day of arresto mayor, as minimum, to one year and one day of prision correccional, as maximum'

Court's reasoning quoted: documents required to enable reviewing courts to resolve whether to give due course; failure 'hinders the review of cases on the merits'; while form infirmities may be waived in the interest of substantial justice, counsel's 'heavy workload' excuse does not persuade
Petition-for-review-only-on-questions-of-law rule barred the petitioner's non-sterilization factual arguments

stances.claim: While the Court was justified in applying a strict reading of the rules, a liberal-school jurist (like the author) would have voted to remand the case to the trial courts to determine the non-sterilization fact and attribute reckless imprudence — to the doctor, the operating-room nurse, the hospital itself, or all of them.

stances.claim: Trial judges must judge by what is just and humane after due process — not 'vie for popularity instead of independence' nor 'surrender to the mob instead of to the truth based on a fair trial' nor 'judge wickedly to gain fame and favors' — drawing the author's own Oct 16 self-quotation into the medical-malpractice context.

notable_anecdotes: Dr. Agbayani's wrenching handwritten Filipino poem dated June 15 — quoted at length — including 'Mahirap isulat ang kalungkutan… Lasapin ang buhay laya. Mahalin lalo ang mga minamahal nyo' — humanizes the convict before the doctrinal analysis begins.
Dr. Agbayani's death of cardiac arrest four and a half months into confinement on Oct 5, 2023 — pivotal biographical fact reframing what would otherwise be a routine procedural-collapse case.

The family's posthumous retention of 'super lawyer Estelito P. Mendoza' to clear the departed patriarch's name — with the author's reputational endorsement of Mendoza's ability to 'resuscitate the dead cases of his celebrated clients.'
Author's transparency disclaimer ('I have not met him or his kins') — establishing arms-length analytical distance from the family even while endorsing their pursuit.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban traces the sad saga of leading orthopedic surgeon Dr. Benigno 'Iggy' Agbayani Jr., convicted of 'reckless imprudence resulting in serious physical injuries' for performing arthroscopy on the left knee of Atty. Saul Q. Hofileña Jr. with an unsterilized arthroscope. Dr. Agbayani died of cardiac arrest on Oct 5, 2023, four and a half months into his confinement, still professing innocence and lamenting what his family, colleagues, and friends consider a 'travesty of justice'; the column quotes at length his wrenching handwritten Filipino poem dated June 15. The procedural history is a cascade of counsel failures: the MTC-Manila convicted him on July 29, 2013; the RTC-Manila dismissed his appeal for counsel's failure to file an appeal memorandum within the 15-day reglementary period despite an extension; the Court of Appeals junked his appeal for failure to append the required documents under the Rules of Court (witnesses' affidavits, prosecution evidence, all prior pleadings); and the SC Third Division, by unsigned extended resolution (UER) on June 23, 2021, denied his petition for review for the same documentary failure -- while shortening his sentence to one month and one day of arresto mayor to one year and one day of prision correccional. The Court explained that the required documents enable the reviewing courts to resolve whether to give due course; though form infirmities may be waived in the interest of substantial justice, counsel's 'heavy workload' excuse 'does not persuade.' The author notes that the petitioner's non-sterilization arguments were barred by the rule that SC petitions for review dwell only on questions of law, not fact, and that the SC majority uses 'the strict or verba legis method of interpretation' (per his Nov 6 column). He places himself in the liberal school of jurisprudence and says he would have voted, if still incumbent, to remand the case to the trial courts to determine whether reckless imprudence occurred and whether it should be attributed to the doctor, the operating-room nurse, the hospital itself, or all of them. He endorses the family's posthumous retention of 'super lawyer Estelito P. Mendoza' to clear Dr. Agbayani's name -- Mendoza's record of resuscitating his celebrated clients' dead cases makes him capable -- but qualifies that the offended party deserves 'justice (not vengeance) in equal measure.' He closes with a doctrinal calming for the medical profession: the UER 'in its present form and language' did not create a precedent on doctor criminal liability for reckless imprudence -- the Court denied the petition pursuant only to existing jurisprudence governing errors or negligence of counsels, and as a rule UERs do not create precedents; only signed decisions and resolutions do.
